Accrual and cash accounting differ in one simple way: accrual records income when you earn it and expenses when you owe them, even if no money has moved yet; cash-basis records them only when cash is received or paid. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/principles-finance-2e/pages/4-1-cash-versus-accrual-accounting?utm_source=openai))

That means accrual shows unpaid invoices and bills, giving a clearer picture of your business’s performance over a period (what you earned and what you owe), while cash-basis shows your actual bank cash at a moment in time and is simpler to keep. ([corporatefinanceinstitute.com](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/accrual-accounting-guide/?utm_source=openai))

Because accrual matches revenue and expenses to when the work happened, larger and public companies report that way under standard accounting rules, and some tax rules require accrual for certain businesses. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/comments/s7-11-13/s71113-117.pdf?utm_source=openai))

If you want simplicity and focus on cash flow, cash-basis can work; for a truer view of profit and obligations, use accrual. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/principles-finance-2e/pages/4-1-cash-versus-accrual-accounting?utm_source=openai))
